headline: Not all technical debt is worth paying. Pay the debt that charges interest.

slides.html:
Not all technical debt is worth paying.

Pay the debt that charges interest.

How to tell the difference — and how to make the case in the language of delivery.

A familiar backlog

The cleanup list that never gets prioritised.

Every team keeps one: the modules engineers dislike, ranked by how ugly they are.

Product sees no customer value and says “next quarter.” The list grows. Engineers stop raising it — and the real problem hides among the cosmetic ones.

Principal vs. interest

Principal — what it would cost to fix the code properly.

Interest — the extra cost you pay every time you touch it: slower changes, more bugs, longer reviews.

Ugly code nobody changes charges almost no interest. Ward Cunningham’s original 1992 metaphor was about exactly this cost of continuing to work on not-quite-right code.
Map debt on two axes

Three debts. One worth paying.

Legacy PDF exporter

Ugly, untested. Changed twice a year. → CONTAIN

Old admin screens

Dated, but simple. Rarely touched. → IGNORE

Pricing rules engine

Changed in most sprints. Each change needs days of manual regression and still ships bugs. → PAY DOWN NOW

Make the case in delivery terms

AREA <module or service>
CHANGES <commits or tickets last quarter>
INTEREST <extra days per change, bugs>
FIX <smallest paydown that cuts the interest>
PAYBACK <sprints until it pays for itself>

“It’s messy” loses the argument. “It costs us two days on every pricing change” usually wins it.

Remember this

Rank debt by the interest it charges, not by how ugly it looks.

Interest only accrues where code changes. Let git history tell you where.

Pay down in slices, inside the feature work that already touches the area.

Which part of your codebase charges the most interest?

And does your backlog know it — in days, not adjectives?
